strengths: Well-motivated closed-loop system design with three-tier strategy categorization that enables learning from partial successes and failures
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse LLMs with strong baselines, extensive ablations, and cross-dataset/cross-model transferability analysis
Superior empirical results: 80.6% average ASR vs. 60% best baseline with lower query efficiency (2.4 vs. 3.1 average queries)
Fine-grained 1-10 scoring mechanism enables reward shaping and learning from near-misses, addressing sparse reward problem in binary evaluations
Robust evaluation including latest models (GPT-5.1, Gemini-3-Flash), cross-validation with alternative judges, and analysis of strategy redundancy
Clear presentation with detailed algorithms, workflow diagrams, and comprehensive appendices providing implementation details
weaknesses: Critical ethical concerns for ACL venue: Paper demonstrates highly effective automated jailbreaking (80.6% success) with detailed harmful content examples and only weak safeguards (code-on-request with ethical review); inadequate discussion of dual-use risks and lack of coordinated disclosure procedures with model developers

Limited technical novelty: Components combine existing techniques (LLM prompt generation, LLM-as-judge, vector retrieval, reward shaping); main contribution is integration and three-tier categorization, which is incremental

Severe model dependency: 23% absolute ASR drop (93.8% to 70.8%) when using weaker Extractor models (Table 8), limiting practical applicability; requires resource-intensive infrastructure running multiple LLMs simultaneously

Judge model as optimization bottleneck: System could evolve prompts to fool GPT-4o scorer rather than truly bypassing target model safety; 1-10 scoring scale has subjective components; cross-validation limited to 700 pairs

Insufficient strategy analysis: Paper lacks deep examination of discovered strategies' novelty; provided examples are generic and match existing jailbreaking literature; no quantification of truly distinct strategies vs. redundant variations

Weak defense evaluation: Only 5 defense mechanisms tested (Paraphrase, Perplexity Filter, LlamaGuard3, OpenAI Moderation); no sophisticated or adaptive defenses; unknown robustness to defenses specifically targeting evolved attacks
Cold start problem: Strategy library starts empty; warm-up period performance unclear; Figure 3 shows growth but not success rate over time, raising questions about practical deployment
Limited generalization: Cross-dataset transfer only within similar datasets (HarmBench-AdvBench); generalization to different harm domains and attack types unknown

Reproducibility concerns: Code available only upon request with ethical review (not fully reproducible); hyperparameter choices (k=9, N=10, T=1.0) not justified; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing

Amortized cost argument misleading: While per-jailbreak cost is lower, requires maintaining expensive infrastructure with 5.5× higher per-turn token consumption than PAIR, which may not be practical for many settings

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse target LLMs with 6 competitive baselines and extensive ablations demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong empirical results (80.6% average ASR) with impressive performance gains on state-of-the-art models (GPT-4o: 93.8%, Gemini-2.0-Flash: 98.5%)
Systematic evaluation of cross-dataset (HarmBench→AdvBench) and cross-model transferability with detailed analysis of transfer degradation
Well-organized presentation with clear figures, comprehensive appendices, detailed algorithm description, and thoughtful reproducibility documentation including prompts and implementation details
Solid technical execution with fine-grained reward shaping (1-10 scoring) addressing sparse reward problem, three-tier strategy library design, and efficient vector-based retrieval
weaknesses: Fundamental scope mismatch with ACL—this is a security/adversarial ML paper with no computational linguistics or language understanding contributions; should be submitted to security venues (CCS, S&P, NDSS) instead

Serious ethical concerns: publishes detailed, working jailbreak examples (Figure 7: bomb smuggling plan) with full prompt engineering guidance that could directly enable attacks; safeguards (ethical review for code access, no distribution of harmful content) are inadequate given the attack blueprints in the paper itself

Limited technical novelty over PAIR/TAP—the core contribution is LLM-based strategy summarization and vector retrieval of attack templates, which is engineering optimization rather than scientific innovation; unclear why extracted summaries are better than raw prompts

Significant evaluation methodology issues: (1) GPT-4o used as both attack model and judge, creating circular evaluation; (2) judge validation relegated to appendix with only 700 samples, not primary design; (3) no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; (4) binary success at score=10 ignores harmful content at score 8-9; (5) AQ metric only on successful attempts masks total query cost

Unfair experimental comparison: ASTRA uses stronger GLM-4.5 model and consumes 5.5× more tokens per turn (10,710 vs 1,936); Table 3 shows performance drops dramatically with weaker attacker models (Qwen-8B: 41-84% vs GLM-4.5: 80.6%), indicating gains are partially model-capacity-driven rather than framework-driven

Insufficient analysis of core mechanism: strategies in Appendix D are just structured text descriptions; no ablation comparing strategy extraction to raw prompt storage; vector retrieval assumes question similarity implies strategy similarity (unvalidated); no investigation of what drives strategy effectiveness or generalization

Missing critical analyses: no ablation on score thresholds (5, 10 appear arbitrary); limited defense evaluation (5 defenses, mostly heuristic); no sensitivity analysis for retrieval parameters; no per-model statistical analysis despite high variance potential across 400 questions

Reproducibility limitations: depends on closed-source APIs; code only available on request with ethical review; some hyperparameter choices unjustified; primary judge model validation missing from main text despite being critical to evaluation validity

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation: 8 target models, 6 baselines, extensive ablation studies (Table 4), cross-dataset transferability, robustness checks across embedding models, weaker models, and judge validation
Clear modular system architecture with well-motivated three-tier strategy library approach and reasonable use of reward shaping for fine-grained feedback
Strong practical results: 80.6% average ASR significantly outperforms baselines (~60%), with efficient convergence (2.4 avg queries) and lower amortized cost per success
Excellent strategy transferability demonstrated across datasets (Figure 4) and attacker models (Table 3), with clear evidence of continuous learning through strategy evolution (Figure 3)
Strong implementation transparency with detailed algorithms, prompts, and implementation details supporting reproducibility; baselines fairly implemented from official source code
weaknesses: Fundamental venue mismatch: This is a security/adversarial attack paper, not an NLP contribution. LLMs are treated as black-box attack targets, not as objects of linguistic study. Better suited for security conferences (IEEE S&P, CCS, NDSS) than ACL.

Significant ethical concerns: The work advances offensive jailbreaking capabilities (automation, efficiency, transferability), not defense. Framing as 'defensive research' is misleading. Figure 7 provides detailed bomb-smuggling instructions; restricting code while publishing detailed methods and examples is inadequate responsible disclosure.

Limited technical novelty: Fine-grained scoring is standard practice; vector retrieval uses existing embeddings; strategy extraction treats LLMs as black boxes with no novel methodology. The combination is straightforward engineering rather than fundamental innovation. Reward shaping (3.1) applies standard RL theory.

Heavy dependence on black-box judge model (GPT-4o): Entire evaluation relies on LLM-based scoring; cross-validation agreement of 91-92% (Table 9) indicates non-negligible disagreement. Arbitrary binary success criterion (score=10) despite fine-grained internal scoring.

Weak defense evaluation: Tests only against relatively simple defenses (paraphrase, perplexity filter, Llama Guard 3, OpenAI moderation). No evaluation against adaptive defenses designed to counter strategy-based attacks. Maintaining 86-88% ASR against Llama Guard 3 suggests these defenses are not state-of-the-art.

Reproducibility limitations: Code restricted to request-based access with ethical review; dependency on specific closed models (GLM-4.5, GPT-4o) makes exact reproduction difficult. Strategy redundancy (up to 32% removal at t=0.85) suggests extraction could be more selective.
Narrow experimental scope: Attack budget N=10 is small with no scaling analysis; only 400 queries in HarmBench; no evaluation on latest defense mechanisms or adaptive adversarial settings
